section_summary: This section contains the end of one copy and a complete second copy of Kilsoo K. Haan’s polemical pamphlet “Japanization, A Peril to Hawaii,” which alleges Japanese political, educational, religious, and military influence in Hawaii and advocates an American embargo and support for China and Korea. It also includes Sino-Korean Peoples League transmittal letters, Office of Naval Intelligence correspondence and translations concerning Japanese consular surveys and defense-related donations, and a State Department acknowledgment. The final pages comprise a cross-reference concerning the Taiyo Maru, a filing slip, and a 1940 New York Evening Post clipping alleging cooperation between Japanese and German propagandists in Hawaii.

subfiles.title: “Japanization, A Peril to Hawaii” — concluding portion
subfiles.about: The concluding portion alleges that Japanese institutions in Hawaii foster loyalty to Japan and urges stronger American action against Japanese expansion.
subfiles.summary: This fragment begins with discussions of the Prince Fushimi Scholarship Fund, Japanese Christianity, dual nationality, and Japanese-language schools. It portrays these institutions as instruments of Japanization and cites Japanese officials and educators in support of that contention. The conclusion connects Hawaii’s security to Japanese expansion across Asia and the Pacific and recommends an embargo on war materials plus moral support for China and Korea.

subfiles.title: Letter transmitting “Japanization, A Peril to Hawaii” to Maxwell M. Hamilton
subfiles.from: Kilsoo K. Haan, Sino-Korean Peoples League
subfiles.to: Maxwell M. Hamilton, Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.about: Haan sends Hamilton a copy of the pamphlet and requests American attention to Japanese activities in the Pacific and Western Hemisphere.
subfiles.summary: Haan states that the pamphlet had recently been presented to members of the Senate committees on foreign relations, naval affairs, and military affairs. He argues that Koreans and Chinese had long warned of Japanese aggression and asks the United States to adopt a positive policy for dealing with Japanese penetration of the Pacific and Western Hemisphere.

subfiles.title: Submission of “Japanization, A Peril to Hawaii” to Senate committees
subfiles.from: Kilsoo K. Haan, Sino-Korean Peoples League of Hawaii
subfiles.to: Members of the Senate Foreign Relations, Naval, and Military Committees, Seventy-Sixth Congress
subfiles.about: The league formally submits Haan’s pamphlet and compares the strategic vulnerability of Guam and Hawaii with Korea’s fate under Japan.
subfiles.summary: The letter stresses Hawaii’s strategic value and cites Laura Thompson’s report that Guam’s inhabitants feared Japanese domination and desired American fortification. It argues that the powers had ignored Korean warnings and sacrificed Korea’s independence, expressing hope that Guam and Hawaii would avoid the same fate.

subfiles.title: “Japanization, A Peril to Hawaii”
subfiles.about: Haan presents an extended argument that Japanese influence and institutions in Hawaii threaten American security and facilitate Japanese expansion.
subfiles.summary: The pamphlet traces Japanese expansion across East Asia and the Pacific, discusses earlier Japanese diplomatic pressure on Hawaii, and describes what it calls “duck diplomacy.” It alleges that scholarship funds, religious bodies, dual nationality practices, consular connections, and Japanese-language schools preserve allegiance to Japan among Hawaii’s Japanese population. The conclusion links these activities to Japanese fortification and commercial ambitions, warning of a possible attack on Hawaii. Haan proposes an embargo on arms and war materials and positive moral aid to China and Korea.

subfiles.title: Naval Intelligence letter transmitting Japanese newspaper translations
subfiles.from: Commander E. B. Nixon, Office of Naval Intelligence
subfiles.about: Nixon forwards translations from Honolulu Japanese newspapers and flags a Japanese airplane-fund donation as potentially relevant to the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: The Office of Naval Intelligence sends the State Department several translations not supplied to any other government department. Nixon specifically calls attention to the report that Hawaii’s Japanese residents had donated nearly 85,000 yen to an airplane fund, suggesting that it might fall under paragraph 3 of the Neutrality Act of May 1, 1937.

subfiles.title: Translations from Hawaii Mainichi and Nippu Jiji
subfiles.from: Office of Naval Intelligence translations of Hawaii Mainichi and Nippu Jiji
subfiles.about: The extracts report a Japanese consular survey in Hilo, an 84,942.23-yen defense donation, and collections of materials and money for visiting Japanese training vessels.
subfiles.summary: One report says the Japanese Consulate asked the Hilo Japanese Society to investigate a wide range of Japanese and Japanese-American organizations. Another records receipt by Japan’s Navy Department of 84,942.23 yen collected on Hawaii for an airplane or national-defense fund, followed by Mitsumasa Yonai’s letter of appreciation. Further extracts describe the division of the consular investigation among local agents and plans to collect metals, textiles, newspapers, comfort bags, and money for the training vessels Nippon Maru and Kaio Maru.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Naval Intelligence translations
subfiles.from: George S. Messersmith, Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Commander E. B. Nixon, Office of the Chief of Naval Operations
subfiles.about: Messersmith acknowledges receipt of Nixon’s letter and the enclosed translations from Honolulu Japanese newspapers.
subfiles.summary: The Assistant Secretary of State thanks Commander Nixon for his June 17 letter addressed to Fletcher Warren. He identifies its subject as translations from Japanese newspapers in Honolulu.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Sino-Korean Peoples League letter concerning the Taiyo Maru
subfiles.from: Sino-Korean Peoples League, Kilsoo K. Haan
subfiles.about: The sheet directs researchers to another file for a letter protesting obstruction of a customs inspection aboard the Japanese passenger ship Taiyo Maru.
subfiles.summary: The cross-reference points to file 611.942/1 for a July 10, 1939 letter from the Sino-Korean Peoples League in Washington. The underlying letter reportedly concerned Japanese officers and the captain of the Taiyo Maru refusing to let Hawaii customs officials inspect a locked safe, and protested their allegedly haughty attitude.

subfiles.title: File notation for 894.20211A/70
subfiles.about: A fragmentary administrative slip records the decimal-file number 894.20211A/70 and the initials PSAB.
subfiles.summary: The page contains no substantive narrative. It preserves only a file designation and administrative initials, apparently serving as a separator or routing slip for the following clipping.

subfiles.title: “Men Against America: Jap-Nazi Propaganda Linked Even in 1938”
subfiles.about: The clipping alleges collaboration between Japanese and German propagandists and portrays Hawaii’s Japanese community as a strategic and political vulnerability.
subfiles.summary: The article says George Sylvester Viereck wrote a 1938 Liberty Magazine article published under Yosuke Matsuoka’s name and presents this as evidence of longstanding German-Japanese ideological cooperation. It describes contacts involving Otto Kiep, Colin Ross, Klaus Mehnert, and Alfred von Wegerer, then focuses on Hawaii as a strategic target and center of Japanese influence. The surviving clipping also discusses Japanese-language education, religious allegiance, bloc voting, visiting Japanese officials, and the Japanese fishing fleet, but portions are truncated.
